title: A shrine where it's taught (section 12)
hookLine: wherever the sutra is taught, the ground becomes like a shrine

cards: A park bench, late afternoon. Pigeons working the gravel. A bus pulls away from the curb.
On the bench, one person reads a few lines aloud from a small paperback, the other listens, and they talk about it for a while. Nothing about the bench changes; there's still gum under the slats.
According to section twelve of the Diamond Sutra, though, something has changed, and it isn't the people. It's the ground under the bench.

teach.b: First, where. Wherever this sutra is explained, the Buddha says, even a verse of four lines of it, that place matters. No temple is required, no particular city.
Wherever. Second, how that place is treated.

The whole world, gods and humans and the beings the sutra calls asuras, should honor that spot as if it were a shrine of the Buddha: a stupa, a caitya, the kind of sacred place people walk around in reverence and bring flowers to.

teach.h: WHERE THE SUTRA IS, THE BUDDHA IS.
teach.b: How much more, the Buddha goes on, someone who can take up the whole sutra, keep it and recite it. Such a person, the sutra says, has achieved something rare and wonderful.

And wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha, or a disciple worthy of honor. Fourth, what makes ground holy. A few days before this sutra began, this path met the book honored, with flowers and both hands.
This section moves from the book to the ground under it. By its measure, holiness isn't in the stone or the roof. It's in what happens there: the teaching explained, out loud, between people.
A kitchen table where someone once explained something good to you.
A hospital hallway where a friend said four right lines. A parked car, engine off, where a real conversation finally happened.

how: In Mahayana communities, places where sutras are recited or taught are treated with respect, and copies of the Diamond Sutra are kept on altars and in high places rather than on the floor.

games.q: what does “a shrine where it's taught” mean?
o: any place this sutra is explained is honored like a shrine
a place is holy only if a copy of the sutra is kept there
only temples built for this sutra count as true shrines

p: as a shrine of the Buddha

s: the sutra says only a temple can become a shrine
wherever it's explained, even four lines, that place is to be honored like a shrine.
in section twelve, gods, humans and asuras honor the place where the sutra is taught
the whole world, the sutra says.
the sutra says the people are holy but the place stays ordinary
it says the place itself is to be honored like a shrine.

games.q: two friends read four lines of this sutra together on a park bench and talk them over. by section twelve's measure, what has happened to the bench?
o: nothing: holy places need a temple.
the ground is to be honored like a shrine.
only the book they read is holy now.
games.why: wherever the sutra is explained, even four lines of it, the sutra says the place should be honored as if it were a shrine of the Buddha.

practice: Feel the room you're in, this floor, this chair, the ordinary air, and bring to mind one place where something true was once said to you or by you.
Let it come clearly, its light, its sounds, and breathe as if you were sitting there now. When you finish, you might touch the floor or the table lightly, the way someone might touch a shrine.

wordCard.voice: A shrine where it's taught. Wherever even four lines of this sutra are explained, the sutra says, that place is to be honored like a shrine. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a shrine or sacred spot, the kind of place this section says the ground becomes.

carryVoice: Your line: the ground becomes a shrine. Even a kitchen table can be one. I'll be here tomorrow.
